Now carries both remaining protocol features (#6954 was merged into this branch); Tasks stays separate (#6956). ## subscriptions/listen (SEP-2575) - New `routes/mcp-gateway/subscriptions.ts`: long-lived SSE stream handled at the route (the SDK transport only does single JSON responses). - Honors `toolsListChanged` only — tool lists are local DB, detected by fingerprint polling (20s); prompt/resource lists are upstream-aggregated, so those types are omitted from the ack per spec. - Ack-first ordering, subscription id (= listen request id) on every notification, graceful-close response, SSE keep-alives. - `tools.listChanged` now advertised `true` for 2026-07-28 clients (backed by the stream); legacy stays `false`. - Legacy clients calling the method get `-32601`; a listen without an id is rejected. ## x-mcp-header (SEP-2243) - New `clients/mcp-param-headers.ts`: annotation validation (token syntax, uniqueness, primitive types, static reachability) and value encoding (decimal ints, lowercase booleans, `=?base64?...?=` wrapper for unsafe values). - Invalid tool definitions are excluded from `tools/list` with a warning; valid annotations mirror argument values into `Mcp-Param-{name}` headers on upstream calls. - Per-call headers ride the passthrough-header pipeline; the existing credential-fingerprint check rebuilds pooled connections when the header set changes, so values can't leak across calls. - Assignment queries now project the tool input schema so the call path reads annotations without an extra lookup. ## Tests / checks - 9 unit + 4 real-socket route tests for subscriptions; 29 unit + 2 transport-level integration + 1 route test for x-mcp-header. - 396 pass across the gateway/client suites; `biome ci`, `tsc`, `knip`, docs link check clean. - Fixes the biome `noControlCharactersInRegex` error that failed #6954's CI (house ignore pattern on the RFC 9110 byte-range regex). ## Docs Gateway page: feature-table rows for change notifications and `x-mcp-header`, plus a client note for subscriptions.","author":{"name":"Joey Orlando","email":"joey@archestra.ai","date":"2026-07-29T14:51:31Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-29T14:51:31Z"}},"author":{"login":"joeyorlando","id":9406895,"profile_url":"https://github.com/joeyorlando","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/9406895?v=4"},"committer":{"login":"web-flow","id":19864447,"profile_url":"https://github.com/web-flow","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/19864447?v=4"}},{"sha":"40fe0314f3c722cb6358c48cd4dbecd3484cc798","html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commit/40fe0314f3c722cb6358c48cd4dbecd3484cc798","commit":{"message":"fix(llm-cost): price the OpenAI Codex models the registry omits (#6957) ## Summary models.dev carries the `gpt-5.3` generation onward but never backfilled the Codex and `chat-latest` models before it. Nothing resolves them, so each one reaches the fabricated default estimate: `gpt-5.1-codex` recorded at $50/M against a published $1.25/M, `gpt-5.1-codex-mini` at $30/M against $0.25/M — a 120× overstatement on a model people run all day. That estimate is not cosmetic. It flows into `interactions.cost`, the cost statistics, optimization-rule savings and token-cost limits. Prices for the eight affected ids are transcribed from OpenAI's own price list and placed at the bottom of the ladder, below the registry. The map can only fill what models.dev omits and cannot override an entry it already carries, so the 62 OpenAI rows the registry prices today cannot move. When the registry catches up the map stops being consulted and can be deleted; a PR adding these models upstream is the follow-up. Every id is stated outright rather than derived by stripping `-codex` to reach a base model. The suffix predicts the price for `gpt-5.1-codex`, which bills exactly what `gpt-5.1` does, and then breaks immediately on `gpt-5.1-codex-mini` at a fifth of it. Inferring a price from a name that resembles a sibling's is the failure this repo already removed once, for the family-matched AWS entries. The proxy's discovery path needed the same fill. It falls back to a first-party registry entry, which finds nothing for these models, so a discovered row kept the estimate for its whole life. That lookup ignores the provider the row was written under: the proxy records a discovered model against the *endpoint's* provider, so naming a Codex model on a Bedrock endpoint produces a `bedrock` row, and a reseller publishing no rate of its own has nothing better to offer than the model's own price. It also covers a second shape. models.dev publishes entries whose `cost` is an empty object, meaning the vendor sets no per-token rate — that entry resolves, so the row was previously enriched with its context and limits while the price alone fell through to the estimate. ## Verification Against the running app, a sync moves exactly the eight rows and nothing else — no row added, none removed, no other provider's price changed: ``` chat-latest 50.00/50.00 -> 5.00/30.00 gpt-5-chat-latest 50.00/50.00 -> 1.25/10.00 gpt-5-codex 50.00/50.00 -> 1.25/10.00 gpt-5.1-chat-latest 50.00/50.00 -> 1.25/10.00 gpt-5.1-codex 50.00/50.00 -> 1.25/10.00 gpt-5.1-codex-max 50.00/50.00 -> 1.25/10.00 gpt-5.1-codex-mini 30.00/30.00 -> 0.25/2.00 gpt-5.2-codex 50.00/50.00 -> 1.75/14.00 ``` The capability matrix carries the three new resolution paths. Its unpriced ratchet consults the published map, so a priced discovery row is not miscounted as falling through — the guard would otherwise quietly lose its meaning. ## Known gap These rows report `priceSource: "models_dev"`, which is wrong; the price came from OpenAI's list. Provenance is re-derived at read time by comparing the stored value against the AWS map rather than recorded when the price is written, so it cannot name a tier it does not know about. That predates this change — it already mislabels 48 Bedrock rows — and fixing it properly means recording the winning tier at write time. Left for that work rather than bolting a half-right label on here. --- ","author":{"name":"Alexander Balashov","email":"22360+divineforest@users.noreply.github.com","date":"2026-07-29T14:42:47Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-29T14:42:47Z"}},"author":{"login":"divineforest","id":22360,"profile_url":"https://github.com/divineforest","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/22360?v=4"},"committer":{"login":"web-flow","id":19864447,"profile_url":"https://github.com/web-flow","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/19864447?v=4"}},{"sha":"7bc0ff3262d277b328cd4d87370cc13193df6b8f","html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commit/7bc0ff3262d277b328cd4d87370cc13193df6b8f","commit":{"message":"fix(a2a): reject contentless message turns instead of sending them to the provider (#6959) ## Summary An A2A `SendMessage` whose only text part is empty or whitespace passed the execute gate but produced no current user turn, so the agent re-sent the conversation's prior context verbatim. Prior context always ends with the agent's last reply, so the request reached the provider terminating on an assistant message. Recent Claude models no longer support assistant prefill and reject such a request with a 400, which surfaced to users as the generic "There was an issue with your request. Please try again." The gate and the executor disagreed on what counts as content: `needToExecute` asks whether any part exists, while the executor builds a current user turn only from text that survives `trim()`. A blank text part satisfies the first and not the second. Blank text parts are now dropped when assembling `messageParts`, so both conditions read the same input. A contentless turn returns the existing `Nothing to execute` error (`-32602`), never reaches the provider, and no longer persists an empty user message into context history. A blank part mixed with real text also stops contributing a stray separator to the joined turn the model receives. Blank text falls through to the file branch rather than returning early, so a part carrying both blank text and a file keeps its payload — otherwise an attachment-only turn would be rejected, since `needToExecute` is evaluated before attachments are collected. Task resumption via `taskOps` is unaffected: it executes through `taskWasSwitchedToWorkingState`, independent of message parts. Known behavior change worth a reviewer's attention: a blank-text turn carrying an ephemeral execution prefix — chatops server-side sessions, where a 1:1 message has no text, no delivered attachment, and no skipped-attachment note — previously executed on the framing alone and now returns `Nothing to execute`. Whether a prefix-only turn should execute at all is unresolved.","author":{"name":"Alexander Balashov","email":"22360+divineforest@users.noreply.github.com","date":"2026-07-29T14:29:43Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-29T14:29:43Z"}},"author":{"login":"divineforest","id":22360,"profile_url":"https://github.com/divineforest","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/22360?v=4"},"committer":{"login":"web-flow","id":19864447,"profile_url":"https://github.com/web-flow","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/19864447?v=4"}},{"sha":"c6782a731c53f3e343ecf3cfdcc818af9d84339a","html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commit/c6782a731c53f3e343ecf3cfdcc818af9d84339a","commit":{"message":"feat(mcp-gateway): stop advertising unimplemented subscriptions, refuse removed methods (#6952) Fifth pass on 2026-07-28, and the one that closes out SEP-2575's transport items. Builds on the directory from #6947. ## The finding that reshaped this PR I set out to make `resources.subscribe` revision-conditional — advertise it to `2025-11-25` clients, withhold it from `2026-07-28` ones. Checking the premise first: **no subscribe handler exists anywhere in the codebase, and no `list_changed` notification has ever been sent.** A client that called `resources/subscribe` always got method-not-found from the SDK, in every revision. The stateless transport has no channel to carry an unsolicited notification even if we wanted to send one. So this was never a revision question. It was false advertising with a real cost: a client seeing `listChanged: true` may cache its lists indefinitely, waiting for an invalidation that never comes — while we've been emitting `ttlMs: 30000` cache hints saying the opposite. The fix is unconditional: - `resources.subscribe` — no longer advertised, any revision. - `resources.listChanged` — now `false`, matching `tools.listChanged`. Freshness is signalled by the SEP-2549 `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` hints on every cacheable result, which is exactly the role the revision assigns them. If the gateway ever grows an event source, `subscriptions/listen` is the thing to build and advertise then. ## Removed-method enforcement `ping`, `logging/setLevel`, `resources/subscribe`, and `resources/unsubscribe` are removed in 2026-07-28 (SEP-2575). A client that **declared** that revision now gets `-32601` with a message saying the method was removed — answering would mean serving a surface the client explicitly opted out of. Legacy clients are untouched, verified route-level: the same `ping` that gets `-32601` under a declared `2026-07-28` header still gets the SDK's automatic pong without one. ## SEP-2575 items closed by analysis, not code - **Per-request `logLevel` in `_meta`** gates `notifications/message` — which the gateway never emits (single JSON response per request, no notification channel). The requirement lands on only half of our flows, which is *why* my first attempt at this looked inert. Dynamically registered credentials are never persisted — `registrationResult` has no consumer outside the OAuth route, so a fresh registration happens on every authorization — and therefore cannot go stale across a server change. That half is satisfied by construction. Operator-configured credentials *do* persist, and those are what this guards: the spec asks for a surfaced error rather than a silent mismatch, since we cannot mint a replacement for a client someone else registered. One deliberate asymmetry: a trailing slash is tolerated here, unlike the byte-exact RFC 9207 response check in #6939. That value is typed into configuration by an operator, so a trailing slash is a typo, not an attack — rejecting it would break working setups for no security gain. CIMD client ids stay portable, since a self-hosted HTTPS identifier means the same thing to every server. **SEP-2164 — emit `-32602`.** We already *accepted* both codes but still sent `-32002` from three sites. The classifier still accepts the old code, so an unmigrated upstream is still read correctly; this changes only what we send. **`resultType` on `tools/call`.** List, read, and discover results already carried the envelope, so a client couldn't rely on it being present everywhere — which is the only thing that makes the field useful. **`notifications/elicitation/complete` removed.** Dropped in this revision: under MRTR a client learns an out-of-band outcome by retrying. Our handler only logged. A `2025-11-25` server that still sends one is ignored rather than erroring. **SEP-414 — W3C trace context.** `traceparent` / `tracestate` / `baggage` read from request `_meta` under the fixed key names, so host → SDK → gateway → upstream can join one span tree. Context without `traceparent` is treated as absent, since the other two only decorate it. ## Testing 369 pass across the gateway, proxy, OAuth, and MCP-client suites. `tsc`, `biome`, `knip` clean. New: 7 unit tests on credential binding, 5 on trace-context extraction, and a route-level test driving the real `tools/call` handler to assert the envelope reaches an ordinary tool result. OAuth mix-up mitigation (SEP-2468, RFC 9207) — the security fix Our callback accepted only `code` and `state`. It had no way to tell *which* authorization server a response came from, because it never received `iss`. That matters here specifically. With one client registered against many upstream authorization servers — MCP's ordinary topology, and the shape the SEP explicitly calls out — an attacker who gets an authorization response from server A delivered to the callback for server B can have the code redeemed at the wrong token endpoint. The authorization step now records the issuer and the server's RFC 9207 advertisement alongside the PKCE verifier, and the callback verifies before the code is transmitted anywhere. **Ordering is the mitigation** — once the code has been sent, the mix-up has already succeeded. Two details worth a reviewer's eye: - **Comparison is exact.** The spec forbids case folding, default-port elision, trailing-slash, and percent-encoding normalization. Each would widen what counts as a match, which is precisely what the attack needs. There's a test per forbidden normalization. - **Absence is handled per the spec's table, not uniformly.** A server that advertised support then omitted `iss` is rejected; one that never advertised it proceeds, so servers predating RFC 9207 keep working. A *present* `iss` is always compared even when unadvertised — the spec's local-policy row, for servers emitting it before updating their metadata. Recording the issuer at authorize time rather than reading config at callback time is deliberate: comparing against a value the attacker may have influenced would defeat the check. ## 2. DCR application_type (SEP-837) Registration now sends `application_type: "native"`. Omitting it defaults to `"web"` under OIDC, which then rejects the localhost-style redirect URIs a self-hosted deployment uses. Non-OIDC servers ignore it. ## 3.   - **Origin Wing**: Explores the earliest genesis commit artifact and founding timestamp.
  - **Chronological Evolution**: Renders an animated timeline of commit artifacts.
  - **Branch Forest**: Maps out historical exploration paths and branches.
  - **Major Artifacts**: Showcases pivotal code relics.
  - **Hall of Fame**: Displays legendary contributors and master artisans.
  - **Forgotten Wing**: Uncovers archived releases and lost exhibits.
- **AI Museum Audio Guide**: Delivers an immersive curator narrative based on real live GitHub data.
